Chess Fine-Tuning Board Probes Report

2026-11-05 · Abhay Anand

Fine-tuning a chess transformer on one grandmaster's moves makes it predict that player better (a crossover in every seed), while the board representation stays intact and causally used; what drifts is mainly the coordinate frame, and the drift largely avoids the board directions.

1. Question

When a policy is specialised on one person's demonstrations, does its internal world state survive? Chess separates the two parts cleanly: Karpov and Kasparov may prefer different moves in the same position, but where each piece stands has exactly one answer.

  • Behaviour: after fine-tuning copies of a chess transformer on Karpov's or Kasparov's moves, does each copy predict its own player better than the other copy does (a crossover)?

  • Representation: does a board probe trained on the base model, then frozen, still read the board from the fine-tuned copies? If it degrades, is the board information lost, or only moved?

This is Direction 3 ("What models represent", board games): probes on frozen representations, with controls that separate real structure from probe capacity. Tools built on a base model (probes, monitors, SAEs) are routinely applied to its fine-tuned descendants, so whether those tools keep working is a practical question too.

2. Setup

One base model, two fine-tuned copies, and a frozen board probe read from all three.

PartWhat we used
Base modelKarvonen's 8-layer, 25M-parameter character-level chess GPT, pretrained on ~16M Lichess games (;1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 ... text)
Fine-tuned copiesAll weights trained, fresh AdamW. Loss only on the target player's move characters plus the trailing space; opponent moves are input only
FairnessSame settings, same number of updates, same target-character budget (~150k each; Karpov's pool subsampled to Kasparov's)
DataPGN Mentor games. Exact name matching (fixed 9 misattributed games). Classical, match, rapid and blitz kept; simuls, blindfold, online, vs-computer dropped
SplitsBy whole game: policy 70% (10% of it dev), probe-fit 10%, probe-dev 5%, test 15%. All 188 Karpov–Kasparov games reserved. 12 near-duplicate test games quarantined
Behaviour metricMean log P of the recorded move (all its characters plus the space), plies 31 onward, identical positions for every model
Board probeLinear map from layer 6 (output of the 6th block) to 64 squares × 13 classes, read at White-to-move dots; fit on the base model plus 3,000 games of 8 other champions, then frozen. Metric: occupied-square error
Settings choicePicked on dev only, rule fixed in advance: learning rate 1e-5, stop at step 60 of a 400-step cosine schedule

Controls.

  • Untrained model: the same probe on a randomly initialised transformer, so input statistics alone can't explain a good score.

  • Control task (Hewitt & Liang): labels set by a fixed random function of the last two moves, so a probe that just memorises scores badly.

  • The other specialist: separates player-specific gains from generic "grandmaster data" gains.

  • Sensitivity test: swap 5–25% of activations with another game's; the metric must detect it.

  • Locked tolerance: 1 percentage point of occupied-square error, set before any result.

3. The board is linearly decodable, and the probe reads the model

On the base model the board appears sharply after block 5: at layer 6 the linear probe gets 96.0% of squares right (12.0% error on occupied squares), the same layer Karvonen reports.

How to read the chart below. x = residual layer (0 = embeddings, k = output of block k−1). y = occupied-square error, lower is better. Blue = trained model, grey = untrained model, solid = linear probe, dashed = MLP probe, red dotted = control task.

  • Trained model: error falls from ~84% to 12% between layers 4 and 6, then rises slightly at the output.

  • Untrained model: never below ~85% (linear) or ~82% (MLP), so the probe isn't solving the task from the input by itself.

  • Control task: flat at chance (≈66.7% of squares right) at every layer, so a probe this size can't memorise its way to a good score.

  • Linear vs MLP: about 4 points apart at layer 6 (12.0% vs 8.0%), so a small part of the board is encoded nonlinearly.

4. Each copy predicts its own player better

On held-out test moves (plies 31 onward), the Karpov copy beats the Kasparov copy on Karpov's moves by +0.0083 nats [+0.0036, +0.0131], and the Kasparov copy wins on Kasparov's by +0.0144 [+0.0074, +0.0219].

ModelKarpov's test moves (11,998)Kasparov's test moves (4,963)
Base−1.9790−1.9399
Karpov copy−1.9224−1.9086
Kasparov copy−1.9308−1.8942

Values are mean log P(played move); higher is better; brackets are game-level 95% bootstrap intervals.

How to read the first chart below. Bars = each copy's gain over the base on each player's moves, with 95% intervals. The crossover is the bar order flipping between the two groups. The intervals overlap visually, but the paired difference (same positions) is significant.

How to read the seed chart. Left: the crossover for every pairing of a Karpov copy with a Kasparov copy (7 × 5 runs: 5 training seeds, plus 2 data subsamples for Karpov). Right: board-probe drift per run at step 60.

  • Robust: the crossover is positive in 35 of 35 pairs on both players (Karpov's moves +0.004 to +0.010; Kasparov's +0.008 to +0.016).

  • Head-to-head games (182, same opponent for both): +0.0150 and +0.0104, so it isn't an opponent-selection effect.

  • Mostly generic gain: both copies improve on both players by +0.03 to +0.06 nats. The player-specific part is about 15–30% of the gain.

  • Interpretable: the Kasparov copy prefers checking moves (−0.020 Karpov-minus-Kasparov on checks vs +0.003 on other moves). In the raw games, Kasparov checks on 8.0% of his moves after move 15, Karpov on 5.9%.

5. The frozen base probe stays within tolerance

At the locked checkpoint the frozen probe's occupied-square error rises from 12.14% to 13.00% on the Karpov copy (+0.86 pp [+0.79, +0.94]) and to 12.66% on the Kasparov copy (+0.52 pp [+0.45, +0.59]); both upper bounds are under the 1 pp tolerance.

How to read the chart below. Left: increase in the frozen probe's error vs fine-tuning step, with 95% intervals (17,478 White-to-move test positions in 645 games); dashed line = the locked 1 pp tolerance. Right: the sensitivity test, swapping a known fraction of activations with another game's at the same move number.

  • The drift is real but small: nonzero and rising with training (+0.10 → +0.34 → +0.86 pp for Karpov).

  • The metric can see damage: swapping just 5% of activations adds +3.5 pp, and 25% adds +16 pp, far above the tolerance.

  • Across seeds (section 4's seed chart, right panel): +0.2 to +0.9 pp at step 60, always under tolerance.

6. What the drift is: moved coordinates, not lost information

At the locked checkpoint a probe refit on each copy loses only +0.10 to +0.22 pp, so the board information is still there; most of the frozen probe's loss is a shifted coordinate frame, and a rotation recovers most of it.

For each checkpoint we read the same test positions four ways:

  • Frozen: the base probe as is (coordinates held fixed).

  • Rotation: the frozen probe after the best rotation from the copy's activations to the base's (orthogonal Procrustes).

  • Affine: the frozen probe after the best affine map.

  • Refit: a fresh probe trained on the copy with the same recipe, which measures whether the information is there at all. Its noise floor is ±0.02 pp.

Checkpoint (Karpov / Kasparov)Policy drift (KL)FrozenRotationAffineRefit
Step 60, locked0.017 / 0.014+0.86 / +0.52+0.29 / +0.01+0.17 / +0.05+0.22 / +0.10
Step 400, same learning rate0.091 / 0.077+0.67 / +0.33+4.2 / +4.2+1.6 / +1.9+2.1 / +2.3
Overfit (lr 3e-5, step 400)0.31 / 0.28+2.9 / +2.1+14.0 / +14.0+5.0 / +5.4+6.2 / +6.4

Error columns are the increase in occupied-square error vs base, in pp. Policy drift = KL(base ‖ copy) per target character.

How to read the decomposition chart. x = how far the policy moved (log scale). y = error increase. One colour per readout; solid = the lr 1e-5 run to step 400, dashed = the overfit run; dotted = tolerance.

  • Small drift: every readout is near zero; the frozen probe is the worst of them, and rotation fixes it.

  • Large drift (surprise): the frozen base probe holds up better than rotation, affine maps, or even a refit. The fine-tune makes large changes the board readout doesn't use, and whole-space maps get dragged by them.

How to read the geometry chart. Left: size of the change at each layer, ‖h_copy − h_base‖ / ‖h_base‖. Middle: effective rank of the change. Right: a joint PCA of layer-6 activations from the base (grey) and both copies.

  • Size: at layer 6 the change is 12% of the activation norm at step 60 and about 40% when overfit; it grows with depth.

  • Avoids the board directions: at step 60 only 33–35% of the change lies in the probe's dominant directions (the top 198, holding 90% of its weight), vs 38.7% for a random direction. When overfit it rises to 45%.

  • Not low-rank: effective rank ≈ 207 at layer 6, so there is no single "style direction".

  • Structure kept: distances between positions barely change (representational similarity 0.99 at step 60).

  • Mostly shared: the Karpov and Kasparov changes point the same way (cosine 0.76), the representational version of "most of the gain is generic". The joint PCA shows the three clouds overlapping.

7. The copies still use the board causally

Editing a piece out of the board along the base probe's direction cuts the probability on that piece's moves by the same amount in the base and in both copies (about 18% at medium strength); a random edit of the same size does nothing.

Method: on 400 White-to-move test positions, pick a White knight, bishop, rook or queen with legal moves. Add a vector to the layer-6 activation at the move boundary so the frozen probe reads that square as empty, at three strengths (probe margin 3, 10, 25). Then score every legal move and measure the drop in total probability on the piece's moves.

ModelWeak editMedium editStrong editRandom direction, same size
Base6.1%18.7%43.6%−0.3% to 0.0%
Karpov copy, step 605.7%18.5%44.4%about 0
Kasparov copy, step 605.4%17.2%40.4%about 0
Overfit copies11–18%28–33%48–54%−1% to −5%

The weak edit changes the activation by about 9% of its norm, the strong one by about 48%.

  • Same causal role: at the locked checkpoint the copies respond to the board edit like the base, so the base probe's direction isn't just readable in them, it is still used to pick moves.

  • Overfit copies are more sensitive, not less: heavy training makes the policy lean on these directions harder.

8. Caveats, what would change the conclusion, and what runs next

The player-specific effect is real but small (about +0.01 nats per move) because each copy trains on only ~1,000 games, 0.01% of pretraining; the next run tests the same question with more data.

Caveats.

  • Small data: the copies memorise after about 2 passes, so only light fine-tuning is usable.

  • One base model and one layer: the probe is read at layer 6 only, on one 25M-parameter model.

  • Refit anomaly: at large drift the refit probe does worse than the frozen one; the geometry suggests why, but it isn't yet tested directly (e.g. a refit restricted to the base probe's subspace).

  • Base probe quality: 12% occupied-square error on grandmaster positions from move 16, vs Karvonen's ~1% on shorter Lichess positions.

What would change the conclusion.

  • A refit probe that does no better than the frozen one at the locked checkpoint: information loss, not just moved coordinates.

  • Board edits that move the base's choices but not the copies': the board would be readable but bypassed.

  • Larger-data fine-tunes where board error passes tolerance before the crossover grows: a real trade-off between specialising and keeping the world state.

Second pair, now done. Lichess 1+0 bullet, Carlsen vs Andrew Tang, about 5,400 games per copy. Same pipeline and analyses. Results are in sections 9 and 10.

9. Second pair: Carlsen vs Tang (Lichess bullet)

The same experiment on a pair with five times more data per copy. Data: Magnus Carlsen (DrNykterstein) and Andrew Tang (penguingim1), rated 1+0 games from June 2017 on, so none come from the months the base model was trained on. Games between the two are held out. A move is dropped if the mover had under 10 s on the clock. Each copy gets a matched budget of about 5,400 games. Everything was picked on dev data only: learning rate 3e-6, step 720 (out of a 1,200-step schedule). The base probe was refit for this pair on Lichess and OTB positions that exclude both players; its error is 9.93%.

Own copy − other copy (95% CI)Carlsen's movesTang's moves
Test games+0.033 [+0.029, +0.037]+0.038 [+0.034, +0.042]
Head-to-head games+0.031+0.026
All seed pairs (30)+0.033 to +0.035+0.038 to +0.041

How to read. Bars show each copy's gain over the base on each player's test moves. Each copy gains most on its own player.

How to read. Left: the crossover for every Carlsen-seed × Tang-seed pair; all 30 are positive and tightly grouped. Right: board-probe drift at step 720 for each seed. Red is the frozen base probe; green is a probe refit on the copy. All are within ±0.15 pp, far below the 1 pp tolerance. Data-seed variants only change the larger pool (Tang's), so two Carlsen runs are identical and counted once.

  • Crossover is about 3× stronger than in P1. P1 was +0.008 / +0.014. With 5× more data the copies separate the two players clearly, and the gap holds on head-to-head games neither copy saw.

  • The frozen board probe holds at the selected checkpoint. Drift is −0.11 pp (Carlsen) and −0.01 pp (Tang), and every seed is between −0.15 and +0.07 pp. The sensitivity check still detects a real break: a 5% activation swap costs +3.5 pp.

How to read. x = how far the copy's move predictions have moved from the base (KL). y = probe error vs base, for four readouts: frozen probe, frozen probe plus a fitted rotation, frozen probe plus a fitted affine map, and a fresh probe (refit). Solid = selected lr 3e-6; dashed = 10× hotter lr 3e-5.

  • Drift is a transient bump, not steady decay. Frozen-probe error rises to +0.39 pp (Carlsen, step 100) and +0.28 pp (Tang, step 60), then returns to about 0 by step 400–720. During the bump, rotation and refit stay near 0, so the board information is still there and only its coordinates moved. The hot runs show the same shape, larger: peaks of +0.86 / +1.07 pp, then down to −0.36 / −0.17 pp by step 400.

  • Late in training the frozen probe is the best readout. For Tang at step 720+, the fitted rotation is worse (+0.4 pp) and refit is about +0.1 pp. There is no rotation left to undo, so fitting a map only adds noise. P1's large-drift checkpoints showed the same pattern.

  • Geometry matches P1. At layer 6: relative distance 0.12, CKA 0.996, RSA 0.99, change effective rank 220–234. 33–36% of the change lies in the probe's top 207 directions, vs 40% for a random subspace, so fine-tuning slightly avoids the board directions. The Carlsen and Tang changes have cosine 0.78.

  • The copies use the board the same way the base does. Edit layer 6 along "square empty − piece here" and measure how much probability drops on moves by the removed piece. At margins 3 / 10 / 25: base 3.9 / 10.3 / 30.7%, Carlsen copy 3.8 / 10.2 / 31.3%, Tang copy 3.5 / 9.5 / 28.1%, hot copies 26–28% at margin 25. A random direction gives ≤1.4%.

10. Both pairs together

One table for the base and all four copies: P1's at step 60 and P2's at step 720. Each is scored on all four players' test moves and on both position domains, OTB classical and Lichess bullet.

How to read. Left: gain in mean log P(move) over the base; rows = copy, columns = whose moves; bold = own player. Middle: frozen-probe drift for each copy, read on OTB positions with P1's probe (brown) and on Lichess bullet positions with P2's probe (blue). Right: cosine between the copies' mean layer-6 changes.

  • Most of what a copy learns is the domain, and some is the player. The Kasparov copy gains +0.048 on Karpov's moves, almost as much as the Karpov copy (+0.057). P1 copies gain ≤ +0.007 on bullet moves; P2 copies gain only +0.005 to +0.024 on OTB moves. Player style is the smaller part on top: P1's crossover is about 0.01 and P2's about 0.035.

  • The changes share a common direction. Copies from the same pair have cosine 0.77–0.78; copies across pairs, 0.56–0.61. So the change looks like a part shared by all human-GM fine-tuning, plus a part for the domain, plus a smaller part for the player.

  • The domain-shift explanation for P1's drift is only partly right. Positions from P1's OTB domain do show more drift for every copy: P2 copies drift +0.17 / +0.26 on OTB vs about 0 on Lichess. But P1's copies drift on Lichess positions too (+0.39 / +0.15). The other factor is timing. P1 was stopped at step 60, which is where P2's trajectory has its transient bump. The two pairs also sit at different doses (step 60 at lr 1e-5 vs step 720 at lr 3e-6). Comparing them at matched KL is the clean follow-up.

  • Absolute probe error depends on the probe's training pool. P2's probe, fit on more and more varied data, reads P1's OTB positions better than P1's own probe: 9.3% vs 12.1% on the base. That's why every claim here is a difference from the base under the same probe.

Bottom line across both pairs. At the selected checkpoint each copy predicts its own player better than the other copy does. The frozen base board probe reads its activations within the 1 pp tolerance, and editing along the probe changes the copy's moves as much as it changes the base's. When drift appears, a rotation removes it and it fades with more training. That points to the board coordinates moving, not the board being forgotten.

11. Same policy shift, both pairs, both position types

Section 10 left a question open: did P1 drift more because of its domain, or because of where training stopped? To answer it, I re-scored every training checkpoint of all four copies on both kinds of positions: OTB with P1's probe, Lichess with P2's probe. KL (how far the copy's move predictions are from the base) is measured on those same positions, so copies can be compared at equal policy change.

How to read. x = KL on these positions (log scale). Top row: frozen base probe. Bottom row: a probe refit on the copy, which measures whether the board information is still there. Solid lines = the selected learning rate; dashed = the hot lr 3e-5.

  • All four curves lie on top of each other. At equal KL, P1 and P2 copies drift by the same amount. At KL 0.01 the frozen probe is +0.4 to +0.5 pp on OTB positions and +0.2 to +0.3 pp on Lichess positions, for every copy. So the drift is set by how much the policy changed and where it's measured, not by which players or how much data.

  • OTB positions show about twice the drift of Lichess positions, for every copy. This is the domain effect from section 10. It depends on where you measure, not on which copy you measure.

  • P1 looked worse because of where it was stopped. Its selected checkpoint (KL about 0.015 on OTB positions) sits at the top of the early bump. P2's checkpoint is past the bump.

  • Real information loss starts only beyond KL about 0.04, on the same curve for every copy. P2's copies hardly reach that range: even at lr 3e-5 they stop at KL 0.04 to 0.07, where refit is +0.1 to +0.5 pp. P1's copies reach KL 0.3, where refit is +5 to +6 pp. With about 1k games a copy can overfit far from the base; with about 5k games, at the same learning rate, it doesn't.

Takeaway. One curve of board readout against policy shift describes all four copies. Up to KL of about 0.03 per target character, the board coordinates wobble but the information stays. Beyond about 0.04 the board itself starts to degrade.

12. Playing style: what actually differs between the copies?

Crossover says the copies differ. To see how, I ran every model on the same 7,300 positions and took its probability for every legal move:

  • 1,500 positions from OTB champion games that involve none of the four players

  • 1,000 positions from Carlsen–Tang games

  • 1,200 positions per player, from that player's own test games

From those probabilities come the expected move habits: capture, check, pawn / king / queen move, castling, moving into the opponent's half, and equal trades. Stockfish 17 (every legal move at depth 12; the opponent's replies at depth 8) adds four engine measures:

  • centipawn loss

  • probability of the engine's top move

  • blunders (≥200 cp)

  • moves that leave the opponent only one good reply (best reply ≥150 cp ahead of the second best)

How to read.

  • A: how well the copies tell who played a test game (AUC), using the difference in each copy's log-probability, plotted against the number of moves seen.

  • B: copy minus base for each feature on neutral positions, with 95% CIs.

  • C: one dot per habit. x = how player A's real moves differ from player B's, each measured against the base on their own positions. y = how A's copy differs from B's copy on the same positions.

  • D: how often two models pick the same top move on neutral positions.

  • The styles are detectable from moves alone. From a whole game, the Carlsen and Tang copies tell who played with AUC 0.76 (68% correct), and it keeps rising with more moves. Karpov vs Kasparov levels off at 0.63.

  • On a given position, the two players' copies disagree more than training noise explains. The two players' copies pick a different top move in about 14.5% of neutral positions. Two seeds of the same player disagree in only 3.5% (Carlsen) to 6.5% (Karpov). Each copy differs from the base in 16 to 18%.

  • The biggest shift is shared within a pair and follows the domain. The OTB copies play more cautiously: captures −2.5 pp, moves into the opponent's half −2 to −4 pp, fewer trades and checks. By Stockfish they're also slightly less accurate (+2.5 / +5 cp loss, fewer engine top moves). The bullet-pro copies get more accurate: −4.5 / −5.5 cp loss, fewer blunders. One possible reading of the OTB result is that a shallow engine favours concrete, forcing moves, which those copies now play less.

  • The player-specific part points the same way as the real players. Across the 8 habits, the copy contrast correlates with the real-player contrast: r = 0.85 for Carlsen–Tang (6 of 8 same sign) and 0.66 for Karpov–Kasparov (7 of 8). For example, Carlsen captures, trades and moves into the opponent's half more than Tang, and his copy does too, at about half the size. The real differences in queen and king moves aren't picked up.

  • Examples. In the neutral positions where the copies disagree most, the choices fit the usual descriptions of these players. In one, the Karpov copy prefers quiet king moves (Kg2 / Kh2, about 59% combined) where the Kasparov copy prefers Bh6 or g4. In another, the Carlsen copy takes the pawn (Rxa5, 77%) where the Tang copy prefers Rd4 (48%). These are single positions: illustrations, not evidence.

Why a small per-move difference matters in chess. A game is a chain of choices, so disagreements compound. If two copies pick different top moves 14.5% of the time, then (taking each position as independent) they play the same first 10 of their own moves only about 21% of the time, and the same first 20 only about 4%. After that, the two games reach positions neither would have reached otherwise. Compounding also amplifies noise, though. Two seeds of the same Carlsen copy (3.5% disagreement) still match on only about half of 20-move sequences. So the evidence for style is the per-position gap over the seed baseline, not the fact that the games diverge. Section 13 measures this directly by playing the games out.

Caveats.

  • There are only 8 habit features and one checkpoint per player, so the correlations are rough.

  • The real-player contrast compares different positions (each player's own games), corrected only by the base's expectation.

  • Stockfish depth 12 / 8 is shallow.

13. Rollouts: do the small per-move differences add up to different games?

Section 12 measured disagreement one position at a time. Here each model plays the games out.

  • Setup. 600 shared start positions: 300 neutral OTB positions and 300 from Carlsen–Tang games, all from move 16 on. Each model plays the side to move; the base model plays the other side. Both sides play greedily (the top legal move), for 30 plies.

  • Why this design. The opponent is the same model in every game, so two games can only split on the tested model's own move.

  • Models compared. The four selected copies, a second training seed of each, and the base. Only fair pairs are compared: the two players within a pair (same data budget, domain, learning rate and step), two seeds of the same player (the noise floor), and each copy against the base. P1 and P2 copies are not compared with each other, because they differ in data size, domain and training length.

How to read. Left: the share of start positions where two models' games are still move-for-move identical after k of the tested model's own moves. Dotted = two seeds of the same player; solid = the two players of a pair (pale = repeated with seed 1); dashed grey = copy vs base. Right: how many of the 64 squares differ between the two games' boards after 30 plies (box = middle half, ◆ = mean).

PairFirst move differsIdentical after 10 own movesSquares different at ply 30 (mean)Squares different if the games split
Karpov copy, two seeds6.3%54%7.112.2
Kasparov copy, two seeds5.8%58%6.412.4
Carlsen copy, two seeds2.3%71%4.612.7
Tang copy, two seeds2.3%73%4.512.3
Karpov vs Kasparov copy12.3%32%10.513.3
Carlsen vs Tang copy13.0%29%10.813.2
Same, seed-1 copies (P1 / P2)11.2% / 12.2%31% / 28%10.6 / 10.913.3 / 13.5
Copy vs base (4 copies)13–15%21–24%11.5–12.013.1–13.5

  • The two players' copies split far more often than two seeds of one player. After 10 own moves, Carlsen and Tang copies have played the same game in 29% of starts, against 71–73% for two seeds of either player. For Karpov vs Kasparov it's 32% vs 54–58%. The result repeats with the seed-1 copies (28% and 31%).

  • P2's player gap stands out more against its own noise. The Carlsen/Tang copies are much more consistent across seeds (2.3% first-move disagreement vs about 6% for P1), so their 42-point gap over the seed baseline is larger than P1's 24 points. This matches the identification result in section 12 (AUC 0.76 vs 0.63).

  • One different move really does lead to a different game. Once two games split, by ply 30 their boards differ on about 12–13 of the 64 squares, whatever caused the split: player style, seed noise or base vs copy. What the player difference changes is how often games split, not how far apart they end up.

  • The copies are still closer to each other than to the base. Copy vs base: 21–24% identical after 10 own moves. Both players' copies move the same way from the base (the shared domain part), then apart from each other (the player part).

  • Games stay together longer than independent positions would predict. From section 12's 14.5% per-position disagreement, independence predicts 21% identical after 10 moves; the observed 29–32% is higher, because consecutive positions in one game are correlated.

Caveats.

  • Greedy play shows each model's single top choice; sampling would show more of the distribution.

  • The base model is a weaker opponent than real grandmasters.

  • 30 plies from move 16 covers the middlegame only.

14. Related work and sources

No prior work we found combines a player-specific crossover with transfer of a frozen base board probe; the closest neighbours are below.

  • Li et al. 2023, Emergent World Representations (Othello-GPT): board state recoverable and causally used.

  • Nanda, Lee, Wattenberg 2023, Emergent Linear Representations: the Othello board is linear in a mine/theirs basis.

  • Karvonen 2024, Emergent World Models in Chess-Playing LMs: our base model and probe recipe.

  • McIlroy-Young et al. 2022, Learning Models of Individual Behavior in Chess: per-player fine-tunes of Maia, no probing.

  • Frisoni et al. 2026, Mixture of Masters: per-grandmaster GPT experts, no probing found.

  • Jain et al. 2023, Effects of Fine-tuning on Procedurally Defined Tasks and Prakash et al. 2024, Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: fine-tuning reuses existing circuits.

  • Hewitt & Liang 2019, Control Tasks: the selectivity control used here.

  • Data: PGN Mentor player files; Lichess API game export. Model: adamkarvonen/chess_llms.

Appendix A. Everything that was run

A1. Compute and logging

  • Training and heavy analysis: two shared lab servers. yu-deepsea has 8× RTX A6000; yu-deepz has 2× RTX 3090 and 2× RTX 2080 Ti. A fine-tuning run needs about 12 GB, so each job was pinned to a free card by PCI bus order.

  • Stockfish 17 (official AVX2 release binary) ran on 36 of deepz's CPU cores.

  • On the Mac (M4): figures, the identification test, and this report.

  • Logging: fine-tuning curves and dev metrics are in the W&B project world-model-internal.

  • Code layout: P1 lives at the repo root; P2 lives in exp_p2/ (WC_ROOT=exp_p2 WC_CONFIG=p2). About 50 fine-tuning runs and ~30 GB of checkpoints are kept on deepsea.

A3. Shared model, training, probe and scoring settings

  • Base model: Karvonen's 8-layer, 25M-parameter character-level GPT (lichess_8layers_ckpt_no_optimizer.pt); untrained baseline randominit_8layers_ckpt.pt. Re-implemented in src/wc/model.py with residual-stream access and an edit hook. Context is 1,023 characters.

  • Fine-tuning:

    • Full weights, fresh AdamW (weight decay 0.1), 16 games per batch, 50 warmup steps, cosine schedule, gradient clip 1, no dropout.

    • Loss only on the target player's move characters plus the trailing space. The final move and clock-filtered moves are excluded.

  • Board probe:

    • Linear, on residual 6, at White-to-move positions; 64 squares × 13 classes.

    • 10 epochs, lr 1e-3, batch 1,024. An MLP variant is used only for the layer sweep.

    • Metric: occupied-square error from move 16. The 1 pp tolerance was locked before any result.

  • Move score: sum of character log-probs including the trailing space, plies ≥ 31, the same positions for every model. Confidence intervals come from a game-level paired bootstrap (2,000 resamples).

A5. Problems found and fixed along the way

  • Player identity: loose name matching pulled in other Karpovs and Kasparovs. Switched to exact-name rules (9 games affected).

  • Leakage: 12 near-duplicate test games were quarantined in P1 (13 in P2).

  • P2 probe pool: the first version contained 938 Carlsen OTB games. Rebuilt with name exclusion.

  • Lichess rated filter: it dropped arena games. Removed, since the API's rated flag already guarantees rated games.

  • Second P2 player: Alireza Firouzja had only about 2.4k usable games per copy, so Andrew Tang replaced him.

  • Overfitting: early runs memorised the data (train loss per character 0.42 → 0.025), and dropout 0.1 broke training. Fixed with low-lr sweeps plus early stopping on dev.

  • GPU placement: a launch bug sent every job to one GPU, and deepz's mixed GPU ordering caused out-of-memory errors. Fixed by pinning jobs by PCI bus order.

  • Style comparison: the first copy-vs-player comparison was dominated by engine-calibration effects. Restricted it to move habits and a within-pair contrast.

A6. Reproducing

  • Per experiment: WC_ROOT=<root> WC_CONFIG=<p1|p2> bash scripts/run_exp.sh sweep, then final, seeds and analyze.

  • Then the cross-experiment scripts: 13_joint.py, 09_analysis.py xdom_* followed by 16_matched_kl.py, 17_identify.py, 18_style_positions.py → 18b (GPU) and 18c (Stockfish) → 18d.

A7. What the evidence supports

The board part of the representation survives player-specific fine-tuning, including fine-tuning that changes the policy in ways you can measure. It stays readable by the old probe up to a small rotation, the information is all there, and the model still uses it causally. The rest of the representation does not survive as a simple transform: the best affine map removes only about half the change (residual 15–18% with no map, 7–9% after it), and the change is high-rank (about 220 dimensions), mostly outside the board directions. All of this holds up to a policy shift of about KL 0.03 per target character; past about 0.04, small-data copies begin to lose the board information itself.

A8. Run matrix: what was run on each model

Within a pair the two copies always got identical treatment. The data-subsample runs only change the larger player pool (Karpov in P1, Tang in P2), so for the other player they are duplicates of the main run.
